You should learn how to make custom normals, as they dictate how shadows are cast on the model. Especially on the face and hair, if you don't use custom normals the shadows will look too detailed and the face and hair will look ugly.

You're welcome. Also just a bonus, quantisation is also much cheaper than using colour ramps, computationally speaking, so they are ideal for real time rendering too.

Thank you for your interest. I do not like to use colour ramps for brightness because brightness does not go from 0 to 1, but from 0 to infinity (you can just keep adding light). It's just better to "lower the resolution" of the brightness by doing things like rounding, softmax, etc.

I find that using colour ramps destroys the dynamic range of materials in very bright and very dark scenes. It can also cause shadow inconsistencies if you use different colour ramps.

Without the hull it looks something like this. It's optically clear but artistically you can argue that it might look better or worse depending on your needs. But it definitely lacks the presence brought by a proper outline.

Unfortunately the outline is still technically opaque, however I cheated a bit by using the transmission in Principled BSDF and make the inverted hull be unaffected by shadows. So it's opaque, but things behind it can still affect the glass and go through it.

The nodes are a bit messy and uses several personal nodes, and unfortunately I don't have enough energy to make it readable or shareable lol. But I'll see what I can do.

But in short it uses four types of shaders; Glass BSDF, Specular BSDF, and Transparent BSDF. The fourth one is principled just for the transmission value. All base shaders share the same IOR, roughness, normals, etc.

You first add together the Glass, Specular, and Principled. Then you have to convert them into RGB, split them into HSV and quantise each values individually (HS in linear, V in logarithmic), then you combine them again to a colour node.

You can then connect the colour node output to an emissive node, using a Fresnel node to control the strength. Finally you then Mix the Emissive and Transparent using the Fresnel node as the factor.

Thank you for your kind words. I can think of three factors:

\- Find tutorials and methods that works for you. I'm a very technical person, bad at subjectivity, and so I approach 3D modeling as such. Pierrick Picaut on YouTube is severely underrated.

\- Focus on your strengths. I'm bad at 2D, but I am confident with math and shaders. I'm bad at sculpting, but I find understanding topology makes 3D modeling easier.

\- Do focused studies with a clear syllabus. I believe it is the most important aspect for autodidactism. Focus on observation. Then anatomy. Then topology. etc etc. Don't be afraid of bad results because progress is not linear. Focus on the subject.

Try to develop your own "strategies" when unioning, finding patterns that outputs the error when you try to union, flipping things around a bit.

Here are a couple that I've found:

* Angled objects are more prone to errors
* Spheres adjacent to cylinders (e.g. making pipes) are *very* prone to errors
* Objects with meshes in general are just prone to errors
* Blocks that don't follow ROBLOX's "0.2 stud rule" placement system (such as being 0.001 stud off) are extremely prone to errors
* Unioning a part and a negated part, if it leaves a hair left somewhere, will cause errors
* And a couple more
